findings.title: Cross-org cache key collision risk from using hash()
findings.body: The cache key uses `hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))`. Python's built-in `hash()` for ints is stable per-process but PYTHONHASHSEED randomization affects strings/some types; more importantly hash() is not guaranteed collision-free, and across different processes/workers hashing may differ (not an issue here since ints hash to themselves), but combining org id with a non-cryptographic hash of a short list has real collision risk is low but using str(project_ids) would be simpler and safer. More critically, the cache value is a simple boolean with no versioning: if `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` changes, cached entries for up to 60s will serve stale eligibility, silently flipping which aggregation (count vs sum(sample_weight)) is applied — causing incorrect counts returned to users with no error during the window.

findings.title: Fragile string-based detection of count() usage breaks aliasing and other call forms
findings.body: `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` only matches the exact string `count()` (after lowering/stripping). Any aliased form like `count() as total`, `count(id)`, or columns with extra whitespace inside parentheses won't be transformed, silently leaving regular (non-upsampled) counts for queries that should be upsampled. This is a brittle approach compared to parsing the actual function AST already used elsewhere in the codebase (event_search parsing).

findings.title: Error-focused detection relies only on raw query string containment
findings.body: _is_error_focused_query does a naive substring check for "event.type:error" in the lowercased query string. This will produce false positives/negatives for queries like `!event.type:error` (negation) or `message:"event.type:error"` as literal text, or when combined with OR logic in different environments. This can cause upsampling to be wrongly applied/not applied for the discover dataset, directly affecting event counts shown to users.

findings.title: Upsampling eligibility recomputed/cached per-call despite inline comment claiming otherwise
findings.body: The comment states "This cached result ensures consistent behavior across query execution," but `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` is called separately in `_get_event_stats` for every closure invocation (top events, rpc, standard), including repeated calls in `get_event_stats_factory` for split-decision requests (errors_only_query, transactions_only_query, original query) which use different `query` strings each time. Since `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` depends on `request.GET` query content, not the varied `query` argument passed to `_get_event_stats`, this can lead to inconsistent upsampling decisions between the split sub-queries (e.g. error-only vs full query) even though the comment implies a single consistent decision was cached for the whole request.

findings.title: Silently swallows all exceptions when extracting client_sample_rate
findings.body: `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` catches bare `Exception` twice and silently ignores failures, including type errors from malformed `contexts` structures. This can mask bugs in test setup where sample_rate is silently not set, making test failures confusing to debug, and is overly broad for test utility code that should fail loudly on unexpected input.

findings.title: Test for upsampled count asserts implausible fixed values without verifying actual sample_weight derivation
findings.body: `test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects` asserts `data[0][1][0]["count"] == 10` based on a single stored event with `client_sample_rate: 0.1`, assuming sample_weight = 1/0.1 = 10. This test doesn't verify that `sample_rate`/`sample_weight` is actually computed and stored correctly end-to-end (depends on `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` in factories.py and the `sample_weight` column population), so if that chain breaks the test might still pass with coincidental values 1 or fail with an unrelated error, not clearly diagnosing the upsampling math itself.
